topic: Why old railway tracks had gaps
script: Rail engineers left gaps so trains stayed on straight rails. A crew runs to a sudden summer kink. The track foreman throws a red flag hard. A passenger hears clickety‑clack and frowns. How? First they bolt rails tight, end to end. Hot day comes; the rails push and buckle. So they add small gaps with fishplates at each joint. Safer in heat, but every wheel hits a step. Sun heats the rails; they try to grow and shove. A feeler gauge shows bigger gaps on hot days. Then sparks fly as railways change the plan. They weld rails into long, seamless strings. Crews pre‑stress them to a neutral temperature. Ballast, clips, and anchors hold that length in place. Some gaps stay at switches, bridges, and devices. The clickety‑clack fades on most main lines. Straight rails came from holding length tight. Old rail joints give way to straight welded rails.
